evidence.claim: Across Iowa on town streets the through highway left behind.
evidence.quote: the highway was gradually straightened, leaving many towns off the route.

evidence.claim: Iowa’s Lincoln Highway Heritage Byway crosses farmland from the Loess Hills near the Missouri River to central plains, river valleys and the Mississippi bluffs.
evidence.quote: From the wind-sculpted Loess Hills near the Missouri River to the level plains and undulating river valleys of central Iowa and to the steep bluffs of the Mississippi River

evidence.claim: The route is mostly paved, with gravel loops.
evidence.quote: SURFACE: Mostly Paved, Some Gravel (Gravel loops)

evidence.claim: The Iowa DOT guide highlights historic main streets, bridges and original 1928 markers as features of this National Scenic Byway.
evidence.quote: It’s easy to remember you’re on the Lincoln Highway with historical bridges, signs, original 1928 Lincoln Highway markers

evidence.claim: National Scenic Byway
evidence.quote: the Iowa Lincoln picnicking. Highway Heritage Byway, a National Scenic Byway.

evidence.claim: Established in 1913 as a memorial to Abraham Lincoln, the transcontinental highway linked Times Square with San Francisco.
evidence.quote: The legendary route, America’s first transcontinental improved highway, was established in 1913, beginning at Times Square in New York City and ending in San Francisco. Created as a memorial to Abraham Lincoln

evidence.claim: Its Iowa route deliberately connected downtowns to draw attention to the Good Roads Movement.
evidence.quote: The first path connected as many downtown areas as possible, in order to create awareness about the Good Roads Movement and the Lincoln Highway.

evidence.claim: US 30 took over in 1926, and later straightening bypassed towns.
evidence.quote: When the Lincoln Highway became U.S. Highway 30 in 1926

evidence.claim: After years of lobbying by the revived Lincoln Highway Association, Iowa designated the historic route its first Heritage Byway in 2006.
evidence.quote: After years of lobbying by the LHA, the Iowa Department of Transportation, in 2006, designated the Lincoln Highway the first Iowa Heritage Byway.

evidence.claim: later straightening bypassed towns
evidence.quote: the highway was gradually straightened, leaving many towns off the route.

evidence.claim: the revived Lincoln Highway Association
evidence.quote: In 1992, the Lincoln Highway Association was reformed

evidence.claim: Travel east from Council Bluffs through Carroll toward Boone and Ames.
evidence.quote: Major Iowa cities along the route include Council Bluffs, Carroll, Boone, Ames, Marshalltown, GETTING OUT Cedar Rapids and Clinton.

evidence.claim: South of Boone, Ledges State Park offers a sandstone gorge; at Colo, Reed-Niland Corner marks the Lincoln and Jefferson highways’ junction.
evidence.quote: The park contains a sandstone gorge carved by Pea's Creek

evidence.claim: Continue through Marshalltown and Cedar Rapids to Mount Vernon, then through the eastern towns toward Clinton.
evidence.quote: Major Iowa cities along the route include Council Bluffs, Carroll, Boone, Ames, Marshalltown, GETTING OUT Cedar Rapids and Clinton.

evidence.claim: Mount Vernon’s uptown and Cornell College occupy opposite ends of a wind-shaped ridge.
evidence.quote: Uptown Mount Vernon is aligned with the southeast end of the ridge crest, while the campus of Cornell College crowns the northwest end of the ridge.

evidence.claim: South of Boone
evidence.quote: south of the city of Boone.

evidence.claim: at Colo, Reed-Niland Corner marks the Lincoln and Jefferson highways’ junction
evidence.quote: The Reed-Niland Corner is a historic "One-Stop" gas station complex located in Colo, Iowa. The complex is located on the junction of the Lincoln Highway and the Jefferson Highway.

evidence.claim: wind-shaped ridge
evidence.quote: a ridge formed of sand and loess along the line of the prevailing wind during the ice ages.

evidence.claim: Pea’s Creek cuts a sandstone gorge south of Boone, reaching 100 feet deep in places.
evidence.quote: The park contains a sandstone gorge carved by Pea's Creek, a tributary of the Des Moines River. The gorge is 100 feet (30 m) deep in places

evidence.claim: Concretions project from its cliffs, and the park contains stone buildings and bridges constructed by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s.
evidence.quote: with concretions jutting from the cliffs.

evidence.claim: Water has also changed the lower park: repeated flooding associated with Saylorville Lake has reduced timbered areas and left silt behind.
evidence.quote: The repeated flooding has radically changed the appearance of the lower Ledges—the timbered areas have been greatly reduced, are often covered with silt.

evidence.claim: A pole in the lowlands records past flood levels.
evidence.quote: There is a flood pole located in the lowlands of the park which has recorded the various flood levels over the years.

evidence.claim: Even the largest recorded floods cover only a small portion of the park.
evidence.quote: even the largest floods on record only submerge a small portion of the park.

evidence.claim: stone buildings and bridges constructed by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s
evidence.quote: The park includes numerous stone buildings and bridges constructed in the 1930s by the Civilian Conservation Corps.

evidence.claim: repeated flooding associated with Saylorville Lake
evidence.quote: In the 1970s, the state created a dam to form Saylorville Lake on the Des Moines River. This action has resulted in repeated flooding of low-lying areas of the park for decades.

evidence.claim: Gas, food and a bed came together at the crossing of the Lincoln and Jefferson highways in Colo.
evidence.quote: The corner consists of a historic gas station, Niland's Cafe, and the Colo Motel.

evidence.claim: Farmer Charlie Reed began with a gas station in 1923, then added cabins for travelers.
evidence.quote: Beginning life as a mere gas station in 1923 on the southeast corner of the property of local farmer Charlie Reed

evidence.claim: A lunch stand became a cafe in 1926 with help from his nephew C. Reed Niland.
evidence.quote: A lunch stand turned cafe was built on the complex in 1926 with the help of Reed's nephew C. Reed Niland.

evidence.claim: During the 1920s and early 1930s, the cafe and station were among the Lincoln Highway’s few round-the-clock stops.
evidence.quote: During the 1920s and early 1930s, the cafe and gas station at Reed/Niland corner was one of only a handful of stops open 24 hours a day along the Lincoln Highway.

evidence.claim: A motel replaced the cabins in 1947; Reed’s gas station now serves as a museum.
evidence.quote: The cabins at the corner were replaced in 1947 by a motel.

evidence.claim: then added cabins for travelers
evidence.quote: soon after added cabins onto the property to accommodate travelers.

evidence.claim: Reed’s gas station now serves as a museum
evidence.quote: Charlie Reed's gas station has been converted into a museum

evidence.claim: Mount Vernon’s “mountain” is a paha: a ridge of sand and loess formed along the prevailing wind during the ice ages.
evidence.quote: This "mountain" is actually a paha, a ridge formed of sand and loess along the line of the prevailing wind during the ice ages.

evidence.claim: It rises up to 100 feet above the surrounding country, with uptown at its southeast end and Cornell College to the northwest.
evidence.quote: rising up to 100 feet (30 m) above the surrounding landscape. Uptown Mount Vernon is aligned with the southeast end of the ridge crest, while the campus of Cornell College crowns the northwest end of the ridge.

evidence.claim: Travelers stopped here before the Lincoln Highway existed.
evidence.quote: its origins date back to at least 1838, when it was known as Pinhook, a rest stop on Military Road

evidence.claim: By 1838, the settlement was known as Pinhook, a stop on the Military Road between Dubuque and Iowa City.
evidence.quote: its origins date back to at least 1838, when it was known as Pinhook, a rest stop on Military Road, which ran between Dubuque, on the Mississippi River, and Iowa City.

evidence.claim: It took the name Mount Vernon in 1847, honoring George Washington’s estate.
evidence.quote: It was renamed Mount Vernon in 1847, after the estate of George Washington.

evidence.claim: Straightening began in the 1930s; later, long stretches of US 30 became a four-lane expressway as traffic increased. The heritage route preserves a journey through those bypassed communities.
evidence.quote: Starting in the 1930s, the route's alignment began to be straightened.

evidence.claim: long stretches of US 30 became a four-lane expressway as traffic increased.
evidence.quote: long sections of US 30 have been upgraded to a four-lane expressway to accommodate increasing traffic.

evidence.claim: The heritage route preserves a journey through those bypassed communities.
evidence.quote: through many rural communities bypassed when U.S. many places for outdoor recreation, providing plenty 30 was realigned over the years.

evidence.claim: A winding, single-lane canyon road crosses Pea’s and Davis creeks at five points, beneath sandstone walls and bluffs.
evidence.quote: The canyon road, a winding one lane path traverses through Pea's and Davis creeks at five points and offers views of 50-foot-high (15 m) sandstone walls buttressing 100-foot-high (30 m) bluffs

evidence.claim: The cafe and gas station moved to their present positions within the complex in 1930.
evidence.quote: In 1930 the locations of the gas station and cafe where shifted to where they currently are located.

evidence.claim: The ridge runs roughly one mile along a roughly northwest-to-southeast axis.
evidence.quote: The Mount Vernon paha is roughly one mile (2 km) long and 1/4 mile (1/2 km) wide, aligned along a roughly northwest to southeast axis
